mcqs.question: What determines whether a ReadWriteLock is actually a win over a plain lock?
options: Whether the protected data structure implements the Comparable interface
Whether the lock object is declared static or instance-level
The number of threads in the JVM's thread pool, regardless of what they do
Whether reads genuinely dominate writes enough that concurrent read access provides real parallelism
mcqs.explanation: The whole benefit hinges on the read:write ratio — plenty of concurrent readers that would otherwise needlessly block each other. Comparable, static vs instance declaration, and raw thread-pool size are unrelated to whether the trade-off pays off.

mcqs.question: In the ReadWriteLock-based cache, what happens when a thread calls put() while three other threads currently hold the read lock via get()?
options: The writer waits until all three readers release the read lock, then holds the write lock exclusively with no reader or writer running concurrently
The writer proceeds immediately in parallel with the three readers
The three readers are forcibly interrupted the moment the writer requests the lock
The write lock request throws an exception since readers are still active
mcqs.explanation: The write lock is exclusive against both readers and other writers, so it must wait for existing readers to finish before proceeding alone. It never runs concurrently with readers, doesn't forcibly interrupt them, and doesn't throw — it simply blocks until it can acquire exclusive access.

mcqs.question: Why don't most ReadWriteLock implementations allow directly upgrading a held read lock to a write lock?
options: Because Java forbids any method from acquiring more than one lock type
If two threads both hold the read lock and both try to upgrade, neither can proceed without the other releasing first, which deadlocks
Because write locks in Java can only be acquired by daemon threads
Because upgrading would require restarting the JVM's lock subsystem
mcqs.explanation: Mutual upgrade attempts between two read-lock holders create a deadlock, since neither can get the write lock while the other still holds a read lock — that's the actual reason direct upgrade is unsafe. There's no such lock-type restriction, no daemon-thread rule, and nothing requires restarting the JVM.

mcqs.question: Why can a ReadWriteLock actually underperform a plain lock under heavy write contention?
options: Because ReadWriteLock objects consume ten times more memory than a plain lock
Because Java disables the read lock entirely once write frequency exceeds a fixed threshold
Its extra bookkeeping for tracking concurrent readers and arbitrating writer handoff adds overhead that isn't offset when readers rarely get to run concurrently anyway
Because a ReadWriteLock can only be acquired by a single thread for the lifetime of the program
mcqs.explanation: Under heavy writes, the parallelism benefit for readers rarely materializes, so the lock's extra coordination overhead becomes a net cost compared to a simpler plain lock. There's no such fixed memory multiplier, no automatic read-lock disabling, and a ReadWriteLock is reusable across many threads over its lifetime.
